title: Full Workshop: Realtime Voice AI — Mark Backman, Daily
talk_summary: A hands-on workshop building realtime voice agents with Pipecat and Gemini Live, covering pipeline orchestration, VAD, turn detection, and context management for low-latency speech apps.

takeaways.what_they_do: They run an eval bot that joins the same room as the agent under test, asks a known question, and an LLM judge verifies the answer end-to-end, replacing slow manual runs of 100+ examples per release.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we used to run like more than 100 examples every release just to make sure they work so I just got tired of it because it's very painful and very slow
takeaways.numbers: 100+ examples per release previously run manually

takeaways.technique: Parallel pipeline with failover and context transfer
takeaways.what_they_do: Pipelines can branch into parallel legs and dynamically switch vendor A to vendor B mid-conversation, transferring context, so a single provider outage doesn't kill the run.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you wanted to have say a failover if vendor A goes down you can move to vendor B dynamically even within the same conversation

takeaways.what_they_do: Break conversations into discrete tasks, feed the LLM task-by-task, and delete stale context (e.g. a date-of-birth check) instead of letting it accumulate; optionally summarize out-of-band with a cheap text LLM.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you may actually remove that from the context like completely get it out of there because otherwise it's just cruff that hangs on

takeaways.technique: Cheap local classifier for a routing decision
takeaways.what_they_do: They run a small native-audio classifier (smart-turn) that outputs complete/incomplete and use it to dynamically adjust behavior, rather than calling a big LLM for the decision.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's a native audioin uh classifier that runs an inference on the in input audio and it simply outputs either complete or incomplete

takeaways.technique: Local lightweight component over paid API
takeaways.what_they_do: They run VAD locally with Silero because it is fast and costs a fraction of a percent, while TTS tokens dominate cost; they deliberately keep cheap work off paid APIs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: running that local VAD gives you superior performance and it allows you and it there's not much of a cost hit
